quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: A long descriptive noun phrase still has one true head noun that determines agreement
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The brilliant young violinist from the conservatory ___ every audience she performs for.
quests.completedSentence: The brilliant young violinist from the conservatory amazes every audience she performs for.
quests.grammarRule: A long descriptive noun phrase still has one true head noun that determines agreement
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'violinist', which is singular; all the adjectives and the prepositional phrase just add description. The verb takes -s: 'amazes'.
quests.nativeTip: Several adjectives come before the noun here - find the noun they're all describing.
quests.example: The brilliant young violinist from the conservatory amazes every audience she performs for.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: A long descriptive noun phrase still has one true head noun that determines agreement

quests.grammarRule: A long descriptive noun phrase still has one true head noun that determines agreement
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'tree', which is singular. The verb takes -s: 'provides'.
quests.nativeTip: Strip away the describing words in front of the noun and the phrase after it.
quests.example: The tall old oak tree behind our house provides shade all summer long.

quests.nativeTip: This subject has several describing words plus a phrase - find the one noun they all point to.
quests.example: The newly renovated apartment on the fifth floor has a stunning view of the harbor.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Multiple stacked modifiers (adjective, participial phrase, prepositional phrase) do not change the true subject

quests.grammarRule: Multiple stacked modifiers (adjective, participial phrase, prepositional phrase) do not change the true subject
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'travelers', which is plural; the participial phrase just adds detail. The verb stays in the base form: 'grow'.
quests.nativeTip: This subject has a describing phrase (waiting at the gate) stacked onto a plural noun - work through each layer.
quests.example: The exhausted travelers waiting at the gate for their delayed flight grow increasingly frustrated.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Multiple stacked modifiers (adjective, participial phrase, prepositional phrase) do not change the true subject

quests.grammarRule: Multiple stacked modifiers (adjective, participial phrase, prepositional phrase) do not change the true subject
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'chef', which is singular. The verb takes -s: 'opens'.
quests.nativeTip: This subject also has several layers - trace back to the singular noun at its core.
quests.example: The talented young chef trained in Paris for over a decade opens a new restaurant downtown.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Multiple stacked modifiers (adjective, participial phrase, prepositional phrase) do not change the true subject

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Appositive and prepositional phrases together do not change the true subject's number

quests.completedSentence: The keynote speaker, a renowned scientist from overseas, opens the conference every year.

quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'the keynote speaker', which is singular; the appositive just identifies who that is. The verb takes -s: 'opens'.
quests.nativeTip: The appositive between the commas renames the subject - it doesn't add a new one.
quests.example: The keynote speaker, a renowned scientist from overseas, opens the conference every year.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Agreement follows the very first noun in a long chain of prepositional phrases

quests.ruleExplanation: The true head noun is 'the key', which is singular, despite the long chain of phrases after it. The verb is 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: This sentence has three 'of/on' phrases stacked together - go all the way back to the very first noun.
quests.example: The key to the lock on the door of the old shed is missing.
